synopsis: Klein’s pre-mortem, published in Harvard Business Review in September 2007, asks a team to imagine its programme has failed and explain why, before the project starts [f9659, f16353]. The glossary applies it to virtual validation by imagining an August 2027 safety review board rejection of virtual-testing results and asking what happened; this is a hypothetical exercise, not a reported rejection [f16353]. The corpus found only one direct test: Veinott, Klein and Wiggins (2010), which assigned 178 students to five conditions and found that pre-mortems reduced confidence in the plan more than the alternatives [f9661, f9662]. That evidence has an independence limitation because the test’s authors are linked to the method’s originator [f9663]. Chapter 12 also associates Klein with Goodenough and Weinstock’s 2015 eliminative argumentation with explicit defeaters, which addresses confidence in a safety argument rather than confidence in a plan [f9714, f9662].

relations.note: Both describe Klein’s 2007 pre-mortem as imagining failure and explaining its causes.
Adds pre-project timing and a hypothetical August 2027 virtual-validation rejection.
Reports the comparative confidence outcome of the identified 178-student experiment.
Adds an originator-link limitation to the sole direct test identified.
Qualifies the confidence-reduction finding with the researchers’ link to the method’s originator.
